what-aiops-is-and-is-not.r: An anomaly detector trained on three quiet weeks flagged everything during a busy sales period. Engineers muted it, and a real fault later went unnoticed.
what-aiops-is-and-is-not.x: AIOps helps with anomaly detection, alert correlation, cause hints and remediation, but only on top of good telemetry and change records. Judge tools by measured noise and time-to-cause improvements, and treat output as checkable hints.

anomaly-detection-on-metrics.r: A detector compared each hour with the one before it, so every Monday rush raised a severe alert. Engineers learned to ignore Mondays, and one Monday a real fault slipped by.
anomaly-detection-on-metrics.x: Start with seasonal baselines rather than static limits or complex models: compare with the same time earlier, require duration, set size floors and review alerts. Add models only if they beat this on past incidents.

alert-correlation-and-noise-reduction.r: A full storage volume made dozens of services fail. The on-call engineer got around two hundred alerts and spent the early minutes reading them rather than looking at the disk.
alert-correlation-and-noise-reduction.x: Correlate with labels, time and dependency graphs so one incident shows a likely source with echoes folded away. Use inhibition with care, expire silences and track alerts per incident as a noise metric.

logs-and-traces-finding-patterns-with-ml.r: A new error appeared at a low rate after a release and sat unseen among millions of lines until customers complained. A report of new message templates would have flagged it within minutes.
logs-and-traces-finding-patterns-with-ml.x: Template clustering, new-message reports, version and host splits, trace comparisons and a change overlay find most causes faster than reading raw logs. Structured, versioned logs make all of it easier.

root-cause-hints-and-incident-assistants.r: An assistant blamed the database for an outage and the team lost twenty minutes there. The real cause was a load balancer configuration change that sat low in the list.
root-cause-hints-and-incident-assistants.x: Rank causes from change timing, dependency relations and anomaly size, show evidence with every hint, restrict language models to summaries and search, and keep people in charge of production actions.

safe-automation-and-auto-remediation.r: A cleanup automation ran with an empty path variable and deleted data other services needed. A dry run and a rule to delete only inside a named directory would have stopped it.
safe-automation-and-auto-remediation.x: Automate small, well-understood, reversible fixes first, wrapped in preconditions, limits, verification, audit logs and a kill switch, and increase autonomy only as evidence of correct decisions accumulates.

debugging-and-investigating-aiops-output.r: An assistant blamed a deploy for slow checkout. An engineer rolled back without checking, but a database lock was the cause. The rollback added ten minutes of disruption.
debugging-and-investigating-aiops-output.x: Check AIOps answers like any guess: ask for evidence, test against data and the timeline, keep a person on every action, and record the misses.

telemetry-quality-for-aiops.r: An anomaly detector flagged hundreds of false alarms because the same service had five different names across tools. Normalizing names through a catalog cut noise sharply.
telemetry-quality-for-aiops.x: Most AIOps failures are data failures. Invest in consistent telemetry and ownership metadata before buying intelligence.

forecasting-capacity-and-saturation.r: A database disk was at 70 percent and looked fine, but growth meant it would fill in nine days. A predict_linear alert gave a week of notice and avoided a weekend outage.
forecasting-capacity-and-saturation.x: Prefer boring models you can explain. A line with seasonality, honest error bars and a human review beats an opaque forecast no one trusts.

llm-assistants-for-incident-response.r: An assistant confidently suggested a command that did not exist during an outage. The team added retrieval from the real runbooks with citations, so every suggestion pointed to a source an engineer could check.
llm-assistants-for-incident-response.x: Use models to reduce toil in reading and writing, not to decide. Keep accountability with the on-call engineer, and design so wrong answers are cheap to notice.

measuring-aiops-value-and-avoiding-hype.r: A vendor claimed a 90 percent noise reduction. In shadow mode the tool also suppressed two real incidents. The team kept the useful clustering and rejected automatic suppression.
measuring-aiops-value-and-avoiding-hype.x: A model that does not beat a simple rule is not worth its complexity. Count false negatives as heavily as false positives, because missed incidents cost more than noisy pages.

runbook-automation-and-guardrails.r: An auto-restart script restarted a healthy service fleet because a metrics outage looked like failure. A precondition that checks several independent signals and a rate limit would have stopped it.
runbook-automation-and-guardrails.x: Automation multiplies mistakes as well as work. Earn trust with a ladder from manual to automatic, and make every action visible, limited and reversible.

statistics-for-ops-percentiles-seasonali.r: A dashboard showed a healthy p99 of 320 ms while customers complained. It averaged the p99 of twelve pods, and one pod with a failing disk had a p99 of 2.9 seconds. Merging the histogram buckets and adding a per-pod maximum revealed the slow pod within minutes.
statistics-for-ops-percentiles-seasonali.x: Most detector disputes are really statistics disputes. Agree on percentiles, seasonality handling and minimum sample sizes first, and write them into the alert standards so every tool and team reads the same numbers the same way.

hands-on-anomaly-detection-z-score-mad-a.r: A z-score detector on error rate stayed silent through a real outage because a short spike earlier had inflated the standard deviation about ninefold. Switching to MAD with a five minute minimum duration caught the next outage in two minutes, and the replay became a regression test.
hands-on-anomaly-detection-z-score-mad-a.x: Pick the simplest detector that meets recall and false alarm targets on your own history. Keep the replay set versioned, hold some incidents out for honest testing, and give each detector an owner who retunes it when the system changes.

change-point-and-trend-detection.r: An API service was restarted by the platform every few days and the memory graph looked bounded. A trend fit between restarts showed memory climbing about 38 MB an hour, a heap profile found a cache that never evicted, and the team alerted on time to limit from then on.
change-point-and-trend-detection.x: The start time of a shift is worth more than the alarm, because it is what you compare with the change log. Make detectors emit both, and make sure restarts, gaps and seasonality are handled before anyone trusts a trend.

event-deduplication-grouping-and-suppres.r: An engineer silenced disk alerts for a database host during a migration and set no end time. Three weeks later the disk filled and nothing paged. The team required an expiry on every silence and added a weekly report of active silences.
event-deduplication-grouping-and-suppres.x: Keep rules in version control with owners and review. The cheapest noise reduction is a good rules layer, and it is also the source of the most invisible outages, so review silences and unused rules on a fixed schedule.

change-correlation-linking-incidents-to-.r: Checkout errors began at 14:03 with no deploys that afternoon. A pricing team had enabled a feature flag two minutes earlier, but the flag service was not in the change feed. Adding flags as a source made the correlator list it first and shortened the next similar incident to minutes.
change-correlation-linking-incidents-to-.x: A change correlator is often the highest value AIOps feature per hour of effort. Its quality depends on feed completeness and on recording the true cause of each incident, which gives you labels to tune the weights.

topology-and-dependency-aware-root-cause.r: The web frontend paged first and the first fifteen minutes went to its team. A dependency graph showed checkout and search both failing and both reading from one database whose latency rose first. A runaway report query was holding locks, and ending it cleared the incident.
topology-and-dependency-aware-root-cause.x: Treat topology as a product with owners and freshness checks. Compare catalog edges with trace edges, report the differences, and never present a root cause without the path that led to it.

tuning-alerts-with-data-precision-recall.r: A payments team found that 9 percent of its 412 monthly alerts were actionable and one CPU rule had fired 188 times without ever needing action. They deleted it, added a burn-rate alert for the checkout SLO, and within a month the actionable share passed 60 percent.
tuning-alerts-with-data-precision-recall.x: Make alert quality a standing metric with a weekly review of the worst five rules. Treat every missed incident as a test case, and compare any new detector with the SLO baseline rather than with nothing.

multivariate-and-service-level-anomalies.r: Overall latency looked fine but one customer in twelve saw slow responses for two days. A per-pod baseline never fired, because that pod had been bad since its last restart. Peer comparison flagged it at once, and the pod with a failing network interface was replaced.
multivariate-and-service-level-anomalies.x: Prefer methods that need no training and survive deploys, such as peer comparison and ratios, before reaching for models. Whatever you use, insist on explanations that a responder can check against the graphs.
